summary:
Roraima stands under Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage has been legal across the country since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 removed surgery, hormones or diagnosis as conditions for changing a name and gender marker. These protections rest on national court rulings and national administration rather than on Roraima state statute, and no state-level deviation from them is recorded for a visitor.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity constitute a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. A legal guide for expatriates confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's on entry and in family matters.

The text of the law does not describe routine experience. OutRight International reports that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, most acutely against trans people, and that enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. A visitor to Roraima should expect the national picture as it applies outside the major metropolitan circuits: recognised rights on paper, thinner practical enforcement, and greater social friction than the large-city experience suggests.
tangentialFactors:
The protective provisions exist under visible political pressure. OutRight International records that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so the framework a visitor relies on is contested rather than settled.

Visibility has nonetheless grown. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022, and over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections.

Courts have applied the 2019 provisions to commercial conduct, which matters for nightlife and hospitality: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

Comparative standing within the country is uneven. The expatriate guide from the São Paulo bar association describes São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis as broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.
localsOnly:
There is no third-gender option in national law, but civil-registry entries of 'non-binary' or 'unspecified' have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender as precedent. Recognition on this point remains case-by-case and varies between states.

Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination without surgery or a court order, and trans voters may register under their lived name and identity even before their documents are updated.

Adoption rights for same-sex couples were settled nationally in 2010 and extended to full equality in 2015, and the 2019 equivalence with racism applies to transphobic conduct as well as homophobic conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents how Roraima's courts, police or Public Prosecutor's Office have applied the 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling. Enforcement quality within Roraima itself is unresolved here.

National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed, including self-declaration before a judge and a stated placement preference. No source records Roraima's compliance with that regime or the conditions in its detention facilities; that question is unresolved.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, shelters and public facilities for trans visitors in Roraima is not sourced, as is any hate-crime prosecution recorded in the state.

The scale of the repeal pressure reported in Congress, and whether it produces changes to the national provisions relied on here, is not resolved by these sources; the 2019 ruling is stated as operative.
